<reason>The debate converged: by Rebuttal 2, CON's own regime (mandatory fare-funded injury surcharge paying victims, verified ID, app-collected fines, suspensions, penalties for missed slowdowns) constituted substantially "more legal responsibility" borne by companies when riders injure pedestrians than the status quo. PRO spotted this in A2.1-A2.2 and pressed it relentlessly: the motion says "responsibility," not "fault," and PRO's opening had itself proposed mandatory injury coverage, so the surcharge adoption was a crossing of the motion line, not a trivial reframe. CON's defenses—the funding/fault split (B2.1) and duty-to-city vs. duty-to-victim (B4.1)—were answered directly (A5.2: a duty that writes the victim's cheque is a duty to her; A5.3: CON drifted from "no wrongful act" to conceding "the company's own breach"). CON landed real hits—Q1 forced A4.1's confinement of the presumption to GPS-provable zones, and B4.5 showed PRO's pay-first scheme mirrors CON's collection model and partly dismantled the insurance analogies—but these only damaged PRO's distinctive mechanism, not the motion route, which the text ("more legal responsibility") favors PRO on. PRO's two clipped turns are a genuine execution cost that keeps the margin moderate in an otherwise clear win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.1-A2.2: PRO quoted CON's own surcharge proposal back and identified it as the motion itself, reframing every later CON concession as affirmation; CON never escaped it—B4.1's city/victim distinction was dismantled in A5.2. CON's best counter-hit was B3.1's GPS-margin dilemma, which forced A4.1 to confine the presumption to proven-violation zones.</best_rebuttal>
